theme: Arrest; trials; Peter’s denial; before Pilate and Herod
readingInstruction: Read Luke 22:47-23:25. The arrest, Peter’s denial, the mockery, and the trials before the council, Pilate, and Herod. Notice how many times Jesus is declared innocent.
settingTheScene: Judas arrives with a crowd, and Jesus is arrested at night. He is taken to the high priest’s house while Peter follows at a distance. Before dawn he stands before the council, then before Pilate, the Roman governor, then Herod Antipas, and again Pilate. Luke stresses that Jesus is innocent. Pilate says so three times, and Herod finds nothing worthy of death.
observation: “Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (22:48).
“But this is your hour, and the power of darkness” (22:53).
“And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the saying of the Lord” (22:61).
“And he went out and wept bitterly” (22:62).
“I find no guilt in this man” (23:4).
“Why? What evil has he done? I have found in him no guilt deserving death” (23:22).
“But he delivered Jesus over to their will” (23:25).
interpretation:
Jesus is arrested in the garden. A disciple cuts off the ear of the high priest’s servant, and Jesus says, “No more of this!” and heals the ear. This is the last healing Luke records, and it is for one of those arresting him. Jesus tells the crowd, “This is your hour, and the power of darkness.” Everything is happening by God’s plan, yet the guilt is real.

Peter follows at a distance, and in the courtyard denies knowing Jesus three times. Then the rooster crows, and “the Lord turned and looked at Peter.” Only Luke tells us this. In that look Peter remembered, “and he went out and wept bitterly.” The look was not condemnation but love. Jesus had prayed for Peter, and the prayer was working.

Jesus is mocked and beaten. At dawn the council asks if he is the Christ, and he replies, “From now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God.” They ask, “Are you the Son of God?” and he says, “You say that I am.” They have what they want.

They take him to Pilate and accuse him of misleading the nation, forbidding tribute to Caesar, and claiming to be a king. Pilate asks if he is the King of the Jews and then declares, “I find no guilt in this man.” When he learns Jesus is a Galilean, he sends him to Herod, who has wanted to see him for a long time and hopes for a sign. Jesus is silent. Herod and his soldiers mock him and send him back. “That same day Herod and Pilate became friends.” The powers of the world unite against the Son of God.

Pilate tries three times to release him. “I have found in him no guilt deserving death.” But the crowd shouts, “Crucify him!” and asks for Barabbas, a murderer. Pilate gives in. “He delivered Jesus over to their will.” An innocent man took the place of a guilty one. Barabbas is a picture of every sinner: set free because Jesus stood in his place.
connection: Isaiah 53:7 says he opened not his mouth. Psalm 41:9 and 55:12-14 describe betrayal by a friend. Zechariah 13:7 foretold the striking of the shepherd. Isaiah 50:6 describes the servant who gave his back to those who strike. Psalm 2:1-2 describes the rulers gathering against the LORD and his anointed. Acts 4:25-28 applies that psalm to Herod and Pilate. 1 Peter 2:22-24 says he committed no sin and bore our sins in his body.
application:
Consider Peter. Have you denied Jesus in word or silence? Let his look of love meet you, and weep as Peter did.

Notice how the innocent one is silent. Where do you need to hold your tongue?

Thank Jesus for being your Barabbas substitute.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for being betrayed, denied, and mocked for you.
Confess where you have denied him.
Thank him that he looked at Peter, and ask him to look at you.
